Week
WēK
n. (rendering Hebrew shābua', a seven, and Greek sabbaton in the idiom “the first day of the week”)
From Old English wice, common Germanic, with an underlying sense of turning or succession — the round that comes back to its start. The Hebrew is franker: shābua' simply means a seven, from the numeral seven, so that in Hebrew one does not speak of a week but of a sevening. This matters for prophecy, where the seventy weeks of Dan 9 are seventy sevens, and the unit counted may be years rather than days. The Greek of the Gospels uses sabbaton, the sabbath, for the whole period, reckoning the week by the day that closes it.

Biblical Definition

The week is the one division of time that has no basis in the motions of the heavens. Months follow the moon and years follow the sun, but nothing in the sky marks off seven days; the week rests solely on the creation ordinance, on God's working six days and resting the seventh, and on the fourth commandment which binds the creature to the same rhythm. It is therefore a standing witness against the notion that time is merely astronomical, and a standing testimony to the God who made and hallowed it. Jacob's service for Rachel is measured by it — “Fulfil her week” (Gen 29:27) — and the marriage feast ran seven days. The Pharisee's boast is measured by it: “I fast twice in the week” (Luk 18:12), a piety kept by the calendar and offered to God as a claim. The prophetic sevens of Dan 9:27 set the covenant confirmed and the sacrifice caused to cease within one week, the hinge of the seventy. And in the New Testament the week's weight shifts to its first day: Christ rose on the first day of the week, the disciples came together on it to break bread, and the collection was appointed on it, so that the Lord's Day now stands where the seventh once stood — not the abolition of the ordinance but its resurrection ordering.

Webster 1828 Definition

The period of seven days, resting on no motion of sun or moon but on the creation ordinance and the fourth commandment; closed in Israel by the sabbath, and opened in the church by the Lord's Day, the first day of the week on which Christ rose.

WEEK, n. The space of seven days. The Hebrews reckoned by weeks from the beginning, the seventh day being appointed for rest at the creation and afterward commanded in the law.

2. In Scripture the word answers to the Hebrew shabua, a seven; and in the prophets a week may denote seven years, as in the seventy weeks of Daniel.

3. Feast of weeks; the second of the three great feasts, kept seven weeks after the passover, called also Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day.

4. The first day of the week; the day on which our Lord rose from the dead, and on which the disciples came together to break bread and to lay by them in store. Acts 20; 1 Cor. 16.

5. Unlike the month and the year, the week has no ground in the courses of the heavenly bodies, but stands wholly upon the divine appointment at the creation.

Key Scripture

Genesis 29:27 — "Fulfil her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years."

Daniel 9:27 — "And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate."

Luke 18:12 — "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess."

Isaiah 66:23 — "And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The week is treated as a human convention that may be redrawn for convenience, and its seventh part — the day of rest and worship — is absorbed into labour and leisure until nothing in the seven is set apart to God.

expand to see more

Because the week alone among the divisions of time has no astronomical footing, it is the first thing revolutionary régimes attack. The French republican calendar imposed a ten-day décade and the early Soviet nepreryvka a staggered five-day cycle, in both cases with the express purpose of dissolving the day of worship by making congregations impossible to gather. Both failed and were abandoned, which is itself a testimony. The modern attack is milder and far more effective: the week is left intact on paper while its seventh part is quietly filled with commerce, sport, and overtime, so that the ordinance is kept in name and broken in substance. The creature who will not rest is not free; he has merely changed masters.

A second corruption runs the other way, and the Lord addressed it directly in the parable of the Pharisee: “I fast twice in the week.” A week kept with rigour can become the instrument of self-righteousness, the calendar turned into a ledger of merit presented to God. Both errors miss what the week is for. It was made for man, given as mercy to a creature who must stop, and it points beyond itself to the rest that remains for the people of God, which is entered by faith and not by observance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shābua' is literally a seven, from the numeral, and can denote seven days or seven years according to context. The New Testament idiom for the week is sabbaton, naming the whole from the sabbath, whence “the first day of the week” is literally the first of the sabbaths.

expand to see more

Hebrew shābua' (H7620) — a seven, a period of seven; used of the week of a marriage feast, of the feast of weeks, and of the seventy sevens of Dan 9:24.

Hebrew sheba' (H7651) — seven; the numeral behind the word, itself tied to shāba', to swear, since an oath was sevened or confirmed by seven.

Hebrew shabbāth (H7676) — sabbath, the seventh day of rest; from shābath, to cease, to desist — the day named not for idleness but for ceasing from one's own works.

Greek sabbaton (G4521) — sabbath, and by idiom the week; “the first day of the week” in Mat 28:1 and Act 20:7 is literally the first of the sabbaths.

Greek pentēkostē (G4005) — Pentecost, the fiftieth day; the feast of weeks counted seven sevens from the wave sheaf, the week's rhythm raised to its own square.

Usage

"Of an ordinary period of seven days: the week of a marriage feast (Gen 29:27); the days of unleavened bread."

"Of prophetic sevens of years: the seventy weeks determined upon Daniel's people (Dan 9:24-27), where the unit is plainly not a week of days."

"Of the Christian assembly: the first day of the week, on which the disciples came together to break bread (Act 20:7) and were charged to lay by in store (1Co 16:2)."
